source.source_title: National Consumer Helpline: E-commerce Grievance Guidance

chunks.section_title: Online order not delivered or refund not received
chunks.text: For an online order that was not delivered, arrived incorrectly, or was not refunded, preserve the order confirmation, invoice, payment record, promised delivery date, tracking status, seller details, and customer-support messages. Contact the seller or platform through its official grievance channel, clearly request delivery, replacement, or refund as appropriate, and keep the written complaint acknowledgement or reference number. Do not make another payment to unlock a refund.

source.source_title: National Consumer Helpline: E-commerce Grievance Guidance

chunks.section_title: Escalating an unresolved e-commerce consumer grievance
chunks.text: The Department of Consumer Affairs National Consumer Helpline accepts consumer grievances through its official web portal and helpline 1915. If the seller or platform does not resolve an e-commerce complaint, the consumer can register the grievance with the available evidence and keep the NCH docket number for follow-up. This is consumer-grievance guidance; use cybercrime.gov.in or 1930 when the facts indicate cyber financial fraud rather than an ordinary delivery, quality, cancellation, or refund dispute. Cyber Saathi must not promise a refund or legal outcome.

source.source_title: Citizen Financial Cyber Frauds Reporting and Management System

chunks.section_title: Urgent financial fraud reporting
chunks.text: For a suspected unauthorized bank, wallet, card, or UPI transaction, act promptly. The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal guidance directs victims to call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in. Preserve the transaction screenshot and keep the bank or wallet name, transaction ID, transaction date, relevant account or UPI details, and any acknowledgement available. Do not share OTP, PIN, password, or send more money.

source.source_title: Citizen Financial Cyber Frauds Reporting and Management System

chunks.section_title: After calling 1930: acknowledgement number and the 24-hour portal complaint
chunks.text: The Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre states that complaints about financial cyber fraud can be reported by calling the national helpline 1930, where an official records the details on the complainant's behalf. After the acknowledgement number arrives by SMS, the complainant is required to make a formal complaint on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal within 24 hours using that acknowledgement number. Calling the helpline alone does not complete the complaint.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal Citizen Manual: Other Cyber Crime

chunks.section_title: Phishing and account compromise evidence
chunks.text: For a phishing email or suspected account compromise, preserve original evidence. Save the email as PDF or EML when possible, retain screenshots, email headers, relevant attachments, the suspicious URL, and the approximate incident date and time. Do not delete the original email, header, screenshot, or attachment before you have recorded the evidence needed for a report.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal Citizen Manual: Other Cyber Crime

chunks.section_title: Harassment, abuse, and cyberstalking evidence
chunks.text: For cyber bullying, stalking, sexting, threatening messages, or abusive social-media content, preserve the original chat, message, profile ID, page URL, and screenshots. Platforms may offer reporting or flagging controls under their own policies. The portal manual lists Online and Social Media Related Crime categories for cyber bullying, stalking, sexting, and related reports.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal Citizen Manual: Other Cyber Crime

chunks.section_title: Impersonation, malicious attachments, and device risk
chunks.text: A fake profile or impersonating email can be reported with the relevant profile ID, URL, screenshots, service-provider details, and approximate date and time. The portal manual also warns that malicious email attachments can install malware or capture saved credentials. Preserve evidence and avoid opening suspicious attachments or sharing one-time passwords.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal FAQ: Women and Child Reporting

chunks.section_title: Women and child safety reporting boundary
chunks.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal has a Women and Child reporting section and a Report Other Cybercrimes section. Its FAQ describes anonymous reporting only for specified online sexually explicit content; it must not be presented as anonymous reporting for every incident. For any report, keep the complaint details accurate and complete. If there is immediate danger, seek local emergency help as well as preserving safe evidence.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal FAQ: Women and Child Reporting

chunks.section_title: Evidence a complainant should keep, and how the portal protects it
chunks.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal FAQ lists the material a complainant may keep and upload, including a credit-card receipt, bank statement, online money-transfer receipt, a copy of an email, the URL of a webpage, chat transcripts, a screenshot of a suspect mobile number, videos, images, and any other relevant document. The portal generates a hash value for an uploaded file so the integrity of the digital evidence can be established later. Keep the original material; do not edit or redistribute it.

source.source_title: राष्ट्रीय साइबर अपराध रिपोर्टिंग पोर्टल: अक्सर पूछे जाने वाले प्रश्न

chunks.section_title: हिंदी में रिपोर्टिंग और साक्ष्य
chunks.text: राष्ट्रीय साइबर अपराध रिपोर्टिंग पोर्टल पर महिलाओं और बच्चों से जुड़े अपराध तथा अन्य साइबर अपराध की रिपोर्टिंग के अलग विकल्प हैं। उपलब्ध साक्ष्य जैसे बैंक स्टेटमेंट, ऑनलाइन धन-अंतरण की रसीद, ई-मेल की प्रति, वेबपेज URL, बातचीत की प्रतिलिपि और संदिग्ध नंबर के स्क्रीनशॉट सुरक्षित रखें। किसी पहचानकर्ता की रिपोर्ट को अपराध का प्रमाण न मानें।

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Suspect Repository and Report Suspect

chunks.section_title: Suspicious identifier handling
chunks.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal describes facilities to search or report suspect mobile numbers, email IDs, account numbers, URLs, messaging handles, SMS headers, and social-media URLs. A reported or matched identifier is not proof that a person is a criminal. Cyber Saathi must not claim live access to the portal or return a live match; it can direct a citizen to the official portal and preserve the identifier for review.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Cyber Safety Tips

chunks.section_title: General cyber safety
chunks.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal publishes cyber safety tips for protecting people, data, and devices. Treat unexpected links, attachments, and requests for passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords with caution. For a suspicious but unclear event, do not invent a diagnosis: ask what happened, preserve relevant evidence, and use the official reporting route when the citizen wants to report a cybercrime.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Cyber Safety Tips

chunks.section_title: Parent guidance for grooming and risky online contact
chunks.text: The portal advises parents to discuss online threats such as grooming, bullying, and stalking with children, set clear boundaries for internet and online-game use, and pay attention when a child becomes unusually secretive or defensive about online activity. Help children choose strong privacy settings and tell a trusted adult about uncomfortable online contact.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Cyber Safety Tips

chunks.section_title: Young people: privacy, fake profiles, and stalking
chunks.text: The portal recommends restricting social-media privacy settings, being selective about stranger requests, learning how to block an uncomfortable contact, and avoiding public sharing of personal details. For suspected cyberstalking, reduce location sharing, avoid sharing phone numbers, email addresses, and photographs with unknown people, and keep evidence of repeated unwanted contact.

source.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Cyber Safety Tips

chunks.section_title: Safer devices and child sexual abuse material reporting
chunks.text: The portal advises using passwords or device locks, keeping software updated, and installing apps only from trusted official sources. It says content relating to child sexual exploitative and abuse material should be reported to the relevant social-media service and can also be reported through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal. Do not redistribute harmful content; preserve only the information needed for safe reporting.

source.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

chunks.section_title: Phishing websites and links
chunks.text: CERT-In advises treating unsolicited links and attachments cautiously. Verify shortened URLs before opening them, look for unusual spelling or grammar, use unique strong passwords, and never provide passwords or PINs by email or text. A real-looking website can still be designed to collect banking or personal information.

source.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

chunks.section_title: Fake authority, digital arrest, and package threats
chunks.text: CERT-In describes scams that use fake official calls, legal accusations, case numbers, package-seizure claims, and urgent threats to make people panic. Stay calm, verify a claim through an official channel, do not transfer money under pressure, and do not disclose payment or sensitive personal details to an unsolicited caller or message.

source.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

chunks.section_title: Fake banking apps, phone scams, and remote access
chunks.text: CERT-In warns that a message may push an APK or fake banking app in order to steal credentials or OTPs. Do not install banking apps from social media, text messages, or other unknown sources. For a caller claiming that a bank or service has a problem, contact the organisation through its official channel; do not share login or financial details and do not grant remote device access.

source.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

chunks.section_title: Fake jobs, prizes, and emotional manipulation
chunks.text: CERT-In lists common warning signs in fake jobs and prize offers: unexpected contact, unrealistically high income, pressure to act quickly, and requests for an upfront fee, account top-up, money transfer, or personal and banking details. Verify independently before committing money or information, and do not pay an advance fee to claim a job, reward, or prize.

source.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

chunks.section_title: Payment, loan, and fake trading app scams
chunks.text: CERT-In says a UPI PIN or OTP is not needed to receive money. Be cautious of urgent payment requests, unknown payment links, guaranteed loan offers, and trading apps promising high returns. Use an official app or website to verify a lender or registered broker, and do not transfer funds to a personal account because of an online investment promise.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Smart Kids: Suraksha Guide

chunks.section_title: Children: protect personal information
chunks.text: CERT-In advises children not to share their name, school, address, phone number, photographs, or other personal details online without a parent’s permission. Keep accounts private, accept requests only from people known offline, avoid unknown links and files, and tell a trusted adult if an online interaction feels frightening or wrong.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Smart Kids: Suraksha Guide

chunks.section_title: Children: social-media privacy and location
chunks.text: CERT-In recommends not publicly posting a school uniform, home, location, or routine, and avoiding public location tags and check-ins. Limit social-media visibility to people the child knows and ask a parent before posting personal material, because posts can be used for impersonation, tracking, or manipulation.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Smart Kids: Suraksha Guide

chunks.section_title: Children: phishing and unsafe websites
chunks.text: CERT-In says children should not click links from strangers, open unfamiliar files, or trust messages promising gifts, prizes, or urgent account warnings. Use trusted sites or bookmarks instead of searching for login pages, check addresses for unusual spelling, and tell a parent or teacher about a suspicious message.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Smart Kids: Suraksha Guide

chunks.section_title: Children: grooming and cyberstalking
chunks.text: CERT-In warns that strangers may build trust through games, chats, compliments, gifts, or secret requests before asking for photos or personal information. Do not respond to someone who causes discomfort, block and report the account where available, avoid sharing location or daily routine, and tell a trusted adult immediately.

source.source_title: CERT-In Mahila Raksha: Cyber Safety for Women

chunks.section_title: Digital footprint and location privacy
chunks.text: CERT-In recommends thinking before posting because online material can be difficult to remove. Avoid sharing personal details, travel plans, daily routine, document images, or unnecessary live location. Keep social-media accounts private so that posts are visible only to trusted people.

source.source_title: CERT-In Mahila Raksha: Cyber Safety for Women

chunks.section_title: Passwords, multi-factor authentication, and urgent-message traps
chunks.text: CERT-In advises long unique passwords, multi-factor authentication where available, and never sharing a password or OTP. Do not trust urgent messages asking for money or OTPs; verify the sender before following a link, expand and verify short URLs, and do not give banking or sensitive personal information by phone or online.

source.source_title: CERT-In Mahila Raksha: Cyber Safety for Women

chunks.section_title: Safe mobile apps and permissions
chunks.text: CERT-In recommends locking a phone, downloading apps only from official app stores, applying updates, reviewing app permissions, and removing apps that are no longer used. Do not allow unnecessary access to contacts or the camera, especially when an app came from an untrusted source.

source.source_title: CERT-In महिला रक्षा: हिंदी साइबर सुरक्षा सुझाव

chunks.section_title: महिला सुरक्षा: डिजिटल निशान, OTP और संदिग्ध लिंक
chunks.text: CERT-In के हिंदी महिला रक्षा सुझाव कहते हैं कि व्यक्तिगत जानकारी, यात्रा योजना, दैनिक दिनचर्या और अनावश्यक स्थान-साझाकरण को सार्वजनिक न करें। पैसे या OTP मांगने वाले अचानक संदेश पर भरोसा न करें, अज्ञात SMS या ई-मेल लिंक पर क्लिक न करें, और बैंकिंग या संवेदनशील जानकारी फोन अथवा ऑनलाइन किसी के साथ साझा न करें।

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Awareness Booklet
source.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2023 booklet

chunks.section_title: Vishing and fake customer-care contacts
chunks.text: CERT-In warns that callers may pretend to be a bank, tax office, gas agency, or another trusted organisation and ask for card details or an OTP. Never share OTP, PIN, CVV, card details, or UPI PIN, including to receive money. Use customer-care details from an authorised website rather than numbers found randomly in search results, and review bank statements for irregularities.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Awareness Booklet
source.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2023 booklet

chunks.section_title: Malicious mobile apps and malware warning signs
chunks.text: CERT-In advises downloading apps only from legitimate sites or authorised app stores, not from SMS, email, or social-media messages. Review requested permissions and user feedback before installing an app. Warning signs of malware can include unexpected pop-ups, redirection to suspicious sites, disabled security software, unexplained loss of storage, or messages sent from an account without permission.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Awareness Booklet
source.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2023 booklet

chunks.section_title: Social-media fraud, fake profiles, and child cyberbullying
chunks.text: CERT-In recommends restricting public social-media visibility, verifying friend requests, using different passwords and multi-factor authentication, and never sharing social-media credentials. For a child facing bullying, stop engaging, save chats or messages, do not respond, block the contact, and tell a trusted parent, teacher, or elder.

source.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Awareness Booklet
source.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2023 booklet

chunks.section_title: Image misuse, blackmail, and support for women
chunks.text: CERT-In describes image morphing and fake profiles as risks that can lead to harassment or blackmail. Preserve screenshots and other evidence, use privacy settings and strong multi-factor authentication, report an objectionable post or fake profile through the relevant social-media help centre, and seek support from trusted family or friends rather than suffering in silence.

source.source_title: Reserve Bank of India: Increasing Instances of Payment Frauds

chunks.section_title: Payment-fraud awareness: credentials, SIM swaps, links, and apps
chunks.text: RBI’s payment-fraud awareness circular identifies common fraud patterns: requests for PINs, OTPs, or passwords; SIM-card swapping; links received in messages or email; and spurious apps that access information stored on a device. Treat these as warning signs, do not disclose critical payment information, and verify through the relevant bank or payment provider’s official channel.

source.source_title: Reserve Bank of India: Customer Protection for Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions

chunks.section_title: Promptly notify the bank about an unauthorised transaction
chunks.text: RBI’s directions say customers should notify their bank as early as possible after an unauthorised electronic banking transaction and that banks must provide multiple 24x7 reporting channels. After receiving a report, banks must take immediate steps to prevent further unauthorised transactions. Exact liability and resolution outcomes depend on the applicable directions and the bank’s current policy, so Cyber Saathi must not promise a result.
